description: Proving Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2024.

talks.title: And what if it was hacked? Tactics and Impacts of Adversarial Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Shows how community-shared jailbreak prompts can push a public chatbot into helping build a keylogger and phishing lure.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a business concern: generative AI is speeding up attackers, and a cited industry survey found many executives worried about adversarial capabilities such as phishing, malware and deepfakes. The speaker gives a short primer on how artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and language models relate, then defines adversarial attacks as inputs crafted to make a model behave against its design. A well-known image misclassification example illustrates the idea before the focus moves to jailbreak prompts for chat assistants. These are grouped into categories including prompt injection, prompt leaking, role-play, developer-mode framing, token manipulation and switching to other languages.

The middle of the session is a live demonstration against a commercial chatbot. The speaker first makes a request the bot refuses, then adds a jailbreak persona taken from a public group and gradually builds a simple keylogger, a data-collection server and a phishing email with HTML through conversation alone. Other real-world examples cover a sales bot talked into selling a product for under a dollar, and a prompt that caused a model to reveal its training data. The point is that guardrails can be sidestepped without conventional exploit code.

To close, the speaker recommends educating staff and developers about LLM risks, improving guardrail hardening, and running AI red teaming to see how systems respond to users. Several published AI security frameworks are listed as starting points. The takeaway for practitioners is that any AI feature exposed to users needs monitoring and testing, since new jailbreaks appear constantly.

talks.title: You can be neurodivergent and succeed in InfoSec
talks.teaser: Offers career guidance for neurodivergent people in infosec, covering job hunts, interviews, accommodations and self-advocacy.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an application security engineer who is autistic, opens by describing how neurodivergent people struggle to enter information security. Job postings are often vague, entry is harder without a personal connection, and certifications alone do not solve the problem.

For the job search, the speaker recommends tracking applications in a spreadsheet by company, interview stage, recruiter and salary. Requesting accommodations, such as keeping a camera off after introductions, can reveal how an employer treats its staff. Offers deserve time and a pros-and-cons list, and it is fine to negotiate or decline. Once employed, micromanagement was presented as harmful, with suggestions for asking for specific feedback, requiring agendas for meetings and building self-advocacy skills. Learning styles also vary, so a single fixed course leaves some people behind.

The closing points stressed patience, moving between specialties such as forensics, GRC or cryptography, and the value of trust with a manager. Disclosing a diagnosis is optional. If someone shares that information with you, ask them directly how they want support handled and whether it should stay private. The takeaway is that fit between a person and a team matters as much as the role itself.

talks.title: Unleashing the Future of Development: The Secret World of Nix & Flakes
talks.teaser: Introduces Nix and Flakes as a way to get reproducible, isolated development environments with pinned dependencies.
talks.summary:
The speaker begins with personal frustration. After repeatedly reinstalling a Linux system and rebuilding packages and configuration with fragile scripts, he turned to Nix. He argues that everyday development tooling rarely pushes developers to think about dependencies or security, and presents Nix as a way to manage packages, system configuration and builds through one declarative setup.

The core of the talk covers the building blocks. A Nix derivation describes how to build a package, and every input is verified with a hash, so outputs can be reproduced and checked. Builds run in a sandbox, and the Nix store keeps packages apart from the usual Unix filesystem layout, which allows rollback and garbage collection of unused items. Flakes provide a more modern, self-describing format that makes inputs explicit, allows remote inspection and building, and offers a development shell that brings a project's dependencies into an isolated environment without system-wide installs. The speaker links this to a smaller attack surface, since unrelated libraries are not installed globally. He also notes trade-offs, such as rebuilding a whole package when one component changes, and that flakes remain experimental.

The closing section points newcomers to the installer, the community package repository and the documentation. The main takeaway is that Nix can act as package manager, operating system and build tool together, though the talk offers only a short overview of what the tool can do.

talks.title: Taking D-Bus to Explore the Bluetooth Landscape
talks.teaser: Shows how a D-Bus based Python tool enumerates nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices and probes their GATT services.
talks.summary:
The talk frames the Bluetooth landscape as a sprawling, poorly documented environment where devices are everywhere and many existing command-line tools are outdated. The speaker presents bleep, a Python tool built on Linux D-Bus and the BlueZ library, which enumerates nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices and reads their services, characteristics, and descriptors. Background covers the host controller interface, which can be sniffed but not injected into, and the nested structure of GATT servers.

Live examples included Apple phones and watches, an Intel-flagged device, and a handheld barcode scanner identified through its GATT data. HCI captures were used to check what the tool reported against actual traffic. Several Apple devices disconnected after a read error, which the speaker interpreted as a deliberate protective reaction. Mapping known trouble handles and skipping them let enumeration proceed much further, though some devices still timed out. Changing how the tool presented itself also altered device behavior, including an audio profile that moved headphones to a laptop.

The main takeaways are that manufacturers shape Bluetooth behavior, producing an uneven landscape, and that systematic probing can trigger defensive disconnects. The talk closed with a CTF-style demonstration of brute-forcing a writable characteristic to retrieve a flag, showing basic read and write interaction with a device.

talks.title: An adversarial approach to Airline Revenue Management
talks.teaser: Explains how airline fares, ticketing and revenue management work, and where their pricing logic can be abused.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why the airline industry is structured the way it is. The speaker covers the regulatory backdrop of bilateral air agreements and traffic freedoms, and explains how airlines use revenue management to fill seats and raise earnings. He frames the session as a black-box view built from personal experimentation rather than insider experience.

The middle section walks through published fares, routing rules, permitted mileage limits and advance purchase restrictions. It distinguishes a reservation from an electronic ticket and describes the roles of validating, marketing and operating carriers. Inventory booking classes are shown as the mechanism that caps how many seats each fare can sell. Fuel surcharges are examined as a weak point, with examples of how surcharge rules have been sidestepped by issuing tickets through another carrier or by adding segments. Related practices such as hidden-city ticketing, currency-based arbitrage and mistake fares are also discussed.

To close, the speaker points to agency debit memos as the industry's main enforcement lever. He suggests that fraud and revenue integrity teams could use pricing data and analytics to spot abuse, which ranges from minor gaming to account takeover and seat hoarding. The main takeaway is an introductory understanding of how fares are built and how their rules can break, giving practitioners a foundation for more specialised discussion.

talks.title: A New Host Touches the Beacon
talks.teaser: Shows how a malicious Skyrim mod, triggered by an in-game item, can open a reverse shell and grow into a C2 beacon.

talks.title: GEN-Z Critique on SOC 2
talks.teaser: Walks through SOC 2 compliance, its audit timeline and costs, and where the framework falls short for startups.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short survey of 50 software engineers and tech executives about SOC 2, the audit framework many US companies are asked to hold before signing business customers. Few respondents could explain what it was, and most said they signed off on compliance policies without reading them closely. The speaker treats this gap as the starting point for questioning what the framework is for and what it costs.

The middle of the talk explains the five trust service criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy) and the difference between a Type I report, a point-in-time snapshot, and a Type II report, which tests whether controls work over a monitoring period. A rough timeline covers preparation, an observation window, the auditor's fieldwork and report compilation. One practical tip is to begin with a shorter observation period so control failures surface sooner, then lengthen it later to limit repeated audit spending. Preparing for an audit also requires coordination across engineering, HR, sales and marketing on controls such as access reviews, background checks and incident response.

The critiques cover uneven auditor expertise, which can affect how well evidence is reviewed, and cost, with the audit alone often running from about $10,000 to $50,000 before penetration testing. The speaker notes that SOC 2 covers broad principles and does not make a company unhackable, so teams should keep up code review and application security testing. The takeaway is that compliance is ongoing work, and the report's main value lies in customer trust.

talks.title: Threat Modeling at Scale: More than shifting left
talks.teaser: Explains how security teams can run threat modeling across large organizations by streamlining intake, collaboration, and handoffs.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a short primer on threat modeling, organized around four questions: what is being built, what could go wrong, what should be done about it, and whether the result holds up. The speaker, who leads a threat analysis team, describes the usual obstacles in a large company: developers focused on delivering features, tight release schedules, limited security expertise on project teams, and tooling that rarely supports threat modeling directly.

The core of the talk is how to run threat modeling across many projects without it becoming a bottleneck. Suggested steps include engaging once a design is reasonably settled but before build work begins, and choosing tools that allow asynchronous collaboration, so architects can edit diagrams, leave notes and review changes outside scheduled meetings. Reports should be tailored to each audience, from executive summaries to detailed engineering findings. The process itself should be defined in advance: what warrants a model, how requests arrive, when checkpoints happen, how disagreements escalate, and who owns remediation after delivery. Lightweight consultation summaries can handle one-off questions, and major architectural changes are the trigger for a full model. Findings can be compared against code scanning and penetration test results to spot gaps, and pentest scope can be narrowed to match.

The speaker argues that early threat modeling saves money because fixes are cheaper before production, and that repeated collaboration builds trust between security and development teams. Practical takeaways are to front-load documentation and diagrams, hold retrospectives to find recurring blockers, and present threat modeling as a checkpoint teams can move through rather than a gate. Audience questions covered developer pushback, how to decide when a model is required, and how release gating is enforced.

talks.title: Building a Security Audit Logging System on a Shoestring Budget
talks.teaser: Walks through a low-cost audit logging stack built on OpenSearch, with build-versus-buy tradeoffs and cost and performance tuning.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem: a fast-growing company adds services faster than it adds security staff, and intrusion detection events get lost when there is no central place to store them. The speaker argues for one centralized logging location and compares buying a commercial platform with building one. Buying brings a single vendor contact and possible discounts, but it risks lock-in, scaling claims that do not hold up, slow support on cheaper tiers, and features behind paywalls. Building gives control over data, retention and cost, but it takes weeks of effort and leaves the team responsible for patching and network access rules.

The middle of the talk covers architecture. A simple design sends events from log forwarders into OpenSearch, with a dashboard in front and per-source permissions so that each forwarder can only write to its own indices. A larger design adds a buffer ahead of ingestion to absorb failures and bursty traffic, a second forwarder to smooth the load, and bulk writes of a few megabytes per chunk. Regional clusters sit close to their data, and single sign-on with group mapping controls who can search what. On cost, the speaker recommends hot and cold data tiers, S3-backed storage for data that is rarely queried, spot nodes paired with replicas, shard sizes of roughly 20 to 50 gigabytes, and SSD sizing that accounts for IOPS limits tied to volume size.

The closing section covers upkeep. Index lifecycle policies can move data to cheaper storage automatically, configuration should be managed through GitOps, and periodic access reviews keep permissions tight. The main takeaway is that building can beat buying when a team accepts the ongoing operational work that comes with it.

talks.title: PCR 9: How a simple misconfiguration can break TPM full disk encryption
talks.teaser: Shows how a simple misconfiguration can break TPM full disk encryption.

talks.title: Hacking Trust Establishment
talks.teaser: Explains how trust is built quickly and applied in social operations, sales, staff management and executive support.
talks.summary:
Carrie Randolph, a senior security consultant with a background in Oklahoma state government and a former state CIO, opens by separating two ideas. Trust is individual, a judgment about whether someone is capable and reliable. Psychological safety is a group condition, describing whether people feel free to speak up and take risks. She splits individual trust into cognitive trust, based on credentials and consistency, and effective trust, based on feeling that someone cares.

The middle of the talk turns these ideas into tactics. For social operations she describes pretext calls that lean on empathy, and nonverbal cues such as eye contact, leaning in and mirroring communication style. For sales and staff management she recommends owning mistakes quickly, sharing honest incident stories, and working out what each stakeholder needs, such as building ties with the CFO and HR before asking for funding or enforcement. She also notes that delivery branding and a clipboard can open doors, as an example of how appearance shapes perceived legitimacy.

She closes with the case for trust inside organizations. Staff who feel trusted are more likely to report suspicious activity and to bring forward process improvements. Her example is a team side project that saved 15 minutes a week and led to raises. She ends by challenging attendees to hack a person as well as a system.

talks.title: Intel-Driven Adversary Simulation for A Holistic Approach to Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how threat intelligence guides adversary simulation to prioritize techniques and improve detection in a bank's purple team.
talks.summary:
Carlos Gonçalves, the CTI leader at a large Brazilian public bank, explains how his team uses threat intelligence to decide what a purple team should simulate. Intelligence comes from a threat-sharing network of more than 4,000 entities, open feeds, internal incident response work and malware databases, all loaded into an open-source CTI platform. Analysts link reports, indicators and techniques for each threat, then map the techniques to MITRE ATT&CK.

Because no team can simulate every technique, the bank ranks them with MITRE's Top Attack Techniques method, which weighs prevalence, choke points and actionability. The chosen techniques are run through an open-source campaign tool that records red team actions and blue team outcomes such as detected, blocked or only logged. Heat maps show coverage gaps. The first round, about six months and more than 180 tests run as separate red and blue exercises, saw defense success fall because attackers moved faster than defenders could fix gaps. Gains came from better log collection, tuned detection rules, new tools and policy changes.

Moving to a joint purple team model, with everyone on one call and red advancing only once blue had responded, raised defense success rates. The speaker's takeaways: purple teaming gives better results but moves slower, so it should be balanced with traditional penetration tests. Cross-functional teams, including risk, help drive change, and top techniques need constant reassessment as threats shift. Threat actors serve mainly as a narrative guide, and exfiltration was tested as a technique rather than with real data.

talks.title: CVSS v4 – A Better Version of an Imperfect Solution
talks.teaser: Examines what CVSS v4 changes in its scoring and where the standard still falls short for vulnerability risk management.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, the widely adopted standard for rating vulnerability severity, and at its fourth version. The speaker explains why the earlier release was seen as too coarse, since different flaws could end up with the same score, and how version 4 reorganizes its metrics into base, threat, environmental and supplemental groups. A worked example involving a router vulnerability compares the old and new vectors, showing how the new attack requirements metric and the split between vulnerable and subsequent system impact change the resulting number.

The middle of the talk focuses on the limits of the standard. Severity is not the same thing as risk, and relying only on the base score is a common mistake. Scores suffer from missing context, especially for open source libraries whose exposure depends on how they are used, and from worst-case assumptions that can inflate ratings. Bug reporters sometimes overstate scores for rewards, and fully manual scoring does not scale to large numbers of findings. Maintainer fatigue and neglect add further friction.

To close, the speaker suggests feeding threat and environmental inputs from threat intelligence and asset inventories through automation, and having CVE numbering authorities publish scores with their advisories rather than leaving them to downstream databases. The takeaway for practitioners is to treat CVSS as one severity input among many, to read the specification closely, and to keep the base score from standing in for a full risk decision.

talks.title: Are you content with our current attacks on Content-Type?
talks.teaser: Shows how trusting the HTTP Content-Type from object storage uploads enables XSS and validation bypasses in real products.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that browsers depend heavily on the Content-Type header in HTTP responses to decide how to render a file. The presenters argue that this trust is weak. Attackers used to struggle to set an arbitrary Content-Type, because upload checks looked at file extensions, declared types and file signatures. Object storage changed that, since an object's metadata can hold any Content-Type string, and SDK-based uploads often skip the validation developers assume is handled for them.

The presenters described how they searched for this pattern. A bug bounty target with an unverified S3-backed upload allowed cross-site scripting, though they could not escalate it further. A code search of well-known open-source JavaScript and TypeScript projects returned thousands of hits, most with no validation or weak validation, and some passed the browser-supplied type straight to object storage. Recurring flaws included client-side-only checks that a proxy can bypass, and prefix, suffix or substring tests on the type. They showed how an allow list turned into a regular expression could be defeated by a crafted value, and how a check that only looked at the start of the string could accept text/html after an image type. Examples included the CarrierWave library for Rails, an Electron application and a Chrome extension, where the impact could be higher.

The takeaway is to stop trusting the response Content-Type and instead compare it against an exact match on a known set of values, such as image/png or image/jpeg, enforced on the server. Teams using object storage should treat any metadata they set on uploads as user-controlled input.

talks.title: The Immortal Retrofuturism of Mainframe Computers and How to Keep Them Safe
talks.teaser: Explains why mainframes persist in banking and government, then walks through common weaknesses and hardening steps.
talks.summary:
Mainframes still carry a large share of banking, retail, healthcare, government and transportation workloads, handling enormous transaction volumes with very high uptime. The talk traces their history from early military and census-era machines through unified architecture and virtual memory, and pushes back on the myths that they are outdated or easily replaced by the cloud.

The speaker, a penetration tester who focuses on mainframe engagements, explains how integrations widen the attack surface. Past breaches were described where attackers got in through a wireless network, a web application, or an exposed FTP connection with default settings, then pivoted into mainframe data. A live demo showed a low-privilege user reaching a command shell, failing to read a stored private key, and then retrieving that same file without authentication by altering a request sent to a web endpoint. Common findings across engagements include broken access control, injection flaws, default credentials and weak password policies.

Recommended defenses treat the whole topology as one system, using network controls, logical partitions and an external security manager. Other advice includes blocking unencrypted protocols, applying hardening benchmarks, monitoring logs, auditing identity and access, enforcing MFA and running recurring testing. The takeaway is that mainframes are staying in service for decades, so the systems connected to them need the same scrutiny.

talks.title: Demystifying SBOMs: Strengthening cybersecurity defenses
talks.teaser: Explains how software bill of materials help teams track dependencies, find vulnerable components and manage supply chain risk.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the growing danger of software supply chain attacks, pointing to Log4j as an example where teams struggled to find every application using a vulnerable library. The presenters describe a software bill of materials (SBOM) as a nested inventory of components, their versions and suppliers, comparable to an ingredient list on a food label. They explain why government agencies are pushing organisations to adopt SBOMs for inventory, compliance and faster response to newly disclosed flaws.

The middle section is a walkthrough of generating an SBOM from a container image with an open-source generator from Anchore. The output is exported in the CycloneDX JSON format, and the presenters compare it with SPDX, which focuses more on package-level licensing. A recorded demo then passes the SBOM to an open-source vulnerability scanner, which lists severity and whether a fix is available, and shows how those findings can be added back into a single document.

The closing part covers practical challenges. Different SBOM tools can report different components, since manifest-only analysis may miss what the code actually uses. Vulnerability data keeps changing after release even when the component list is stable, so teams need ongoing updates. Prioritising a long list of findings also requires exploitability context. The speakers encourage attendees to build SBOM generation and scanning into their CI/CD pipelines and to look into exploitability exchange formats.
